question: The EU is facing an acute and ever-worsening demographic crisis, with birth rates below the required population replacement level for many years1.

The increased cost of living, economic uncertainty, precarious employment, the difficulty of securing stable and quality employment, the inability to balance work and family life, and the ever-increasing cost of raising children are important factors that dissuade young people from having children and make it difficult to create and support young families.

The problem is more pronounced in certain Member States such as Greece2, as well as in island, mountainous and remote areas, where declining births and an ageing population, combined with an increasing number of permanent residents who are leaving, especially young people, are all factors that are accelerating demographic decline and leading to depopulation3.
With this in mind, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it plan to propose a European action plan to support families, in particular large families, single-parent families and those in vulnerable situations, as requested by the European Parliament?

How does it intend to support the response to demographic challenges in the provinces, islands, mountainous and remote areas of the Member States with the lowest birth rates and the highest risk of depopulation?
Does it plan to put forward a holistic European strategy to tackle the demographic problem, with mandatory measures, measurable targets and adequate funding?

According to Eurostat figures, the fertility rate in Europe fell to 1.34 children per woman in 2024, which is well below the 2.1 rate considered to be the population replacement level, and the number of births dropped to 3.55 million, the lowest recorded in recent decades. 2 Specifically, Greece has one of the lowest fertility rates among the EU Member States, with 1.

24 births per woman and it has the fourth oldest population in the EU, with a median age of 47.2. What is more, according to the OECD’s ‘Health at a Glance 2025’ report, in 2050 Greece is expected to be the oldest country in the EU (https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/11/health-at-a-glance2025_a894f72e/8f9e3f98-en.pdf).

3 In Greece, at least 51 islands have become depopulated since 1950 and more are expected to meet the same fate over the next 20 years (https://www.naftemporiki.gr/society/1795599/dimografiko-apo-to-1950erimosan-51-mikra-nisia-ti-empodizei-tin-epistrofi-ton-neon-kai-to-paradeigma-tis-tiloy/). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.10.

2026) Although policies related to demographic change are primarily national competences, the EU supports Member States’ efforts through the Work-Life Balance Directive1, the Quality Jobs Roadmap2, the European Child Guarantee3, the European Care Strategy4, the Anti-Poverty Strategy5, the European Affordable Housing Plan6, the EU Youth Strategy7 and the Strategy on Intergenerational Fairness8, which together aim to create favourable conditions for young people and families in the EU.

The Commission is supporting islands, mountainous and remote areas to adapt to demographic decline through initiatives such as the Rural Pact9, the Rural Action Plan10, the Talent Booster Mechanism, the EU strategy for islands11, the EU Strategy for the outermost regions12 and the ongoing work on the Right to Stay13.

EU funding instruments such as the European Regional Development Fund, the European Social Fund Plus and the Technical Support Instrument support Member States in mitigating the impact of demographic change. The proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework includes many references to support Member States, also financially, to face the consequences of the demographic trends that are more relevant for them.
The Commission’s Demography Toolbox14 provides Member States with a set of EU policy tools to address demographic change, in line with EU’s role that is complementary to national competences.

The Commission recently published the 2026 Demography Report15 providing an update on data, statistics and projections on how EU’s population is changing in size, structure and geographic distribution, and exploring the underlying drivers. The Commission monitors and is preparing an update on its implementation.
